Selected studies are compared by label origin, analysis unit, training organisation, protection mechanism and cost boundary. Table 2.1 summarises the core EHR detection studies. Table 2.2 examines the nearest application, Martínez Llamas et al. (2025). Table 2.3 records sample sizes, labels, designs and reported results. Later and adjacent-domain work is discussed thematically below, with source-specific checks in Appendix A.4.

Label origin determines what detection measures can establish. Expert suspicion, investigated misuse, simulated threats and algorithm-generated labels supply different evidence (Boxwala et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2011; Chen & Malin, 2011; Tabassum et al., 2024). Here, supplied scenario labels define threats as positives and routine and unusual legitimate activity as negatives. AP, recall and false-positive rates evaluate that distinction.

Clinical and relational evidence makes legitimate exceptions central to evaluation. Care relationships can explain flagged access (Fabbri & LeFevre, 2011; Hedda et al., 2017); Yeng et al. (2021) include nonmalicious abnormal cases, and Menon et al. (2014) model user–patient relationships. The present design therefore reports errors on routine and unusual legitimate activity separately, rather than treating unusualness as proof of misuse.

The nearest EHR application, Martínez Llamas et al. (2025), combines an LSTM autoencoder, Flower and FedAvg, evaluating reconstruction and flagging without anomaly ground truth. Here, the same model family and framework support a comparison of training workflows, labelled-session outcomes and SecAgg+ cost. Table 2.2 sets out this methodological relationship; Table 2.3 retains the original evaluation details.

Synthetic EHR experiments broaden detector choices: Matos et al. (2026) combine autoencoder scores with supervised and contextual components; Iqbal et al. (2026) evaluate a variational autoencoder; Segar and Vijayan (2026) combine temporal convolution and attention with a blockchain simulation. Their sample counts, event-to-window transformations or partition descriptions leave parts of the evaluation uncertain. Appendix A.4 records these specific reporting limitations, which do not establish that leakage occurred.

The present comparison makes the whole supplied session its evaluation unit, keeps test labels and partitions fixed across training approaches, and reports ranking alongside threshold-specific errors. Repeated scoring does not create additional independent observations. Section 5.7 assesses recurring actors and patients and the documented development access to test structure.

Governance frameworks address authorisation and auditability alongside detection. Sutradhar et al. (2026) integrate context-aware and attribute-based access control, logging, monitoring and Isolation Forest in a permissioned blockchain testbed. This concerns the surrounding access-governance system. Here, the measured change is within federated training: adding SecAgg+ to a fixed detector and evaluation procedure. Appendix A.4 distinguishes the executed testbed from its proposed federated extensions.

Update-protection comparisons depend on which mechanisms were executed. Maghrabi et al. (2026) describe FedAvg, TLS and secure multiparty computation (SMPC), which computes over protected participant inputs. Their available text leaves SMPC’s experimental status unresolved and reports no matched ordinary-versus-secure aggregation experiment. This distinction underlies the present comparison of implemented FedAvg workflows under matched detector, input and training settings.

Broader frameworks combine several detection and protection components. Munusamy and Jothi (2026) join blockchain, federated learning and secure third-party computation in an EHR-security preprint. Javed et al. (2025) address healthcare privacy, security and efficiency. Such integration answers a broader design question than adding one aggregation mechanism.

Component comparisons ask which part accounts for a change. Kamatchi and Uma (2025) separately remove node clustering, global-model generation or authentication from an IoT insider-detection framework. Abbasi et al. (2025) evaluate FedAvg on CERT user profiles with simulated privacy mechanisms. Tanvir et al. (2026) combine IoT traffic and EMR payloads, but remove differential privacy and secure aggregation together in Table 8. That joint removal cannot isolate secure aggregation’s contribution. Here, detector, sampling schedules and round budget remain matched when SecAgg+ is added.

Cost comparisons must identify what changes and what is counted. Shamim et al. (2026) hold detector and cryptographic parameters fixed while changing the encrypted intrusion-detection stack. Qazi et al. (2026) use component ablations, but their headline communication reduction compares different round budgets; Table 20 does not isolate secure aggregation. Here, paired comparisons measure complete training-workflow time and application-message content under the same federated budget.

Lytvyn and Nguyen (2024) provide a closer aggregation precedent: their Flower experiments compare ordinary FedAvg and SecAgg+ with the same model, partitions and settings, measuring network-traffic forecasting errors and training time together. Secure aggregation increased elapsed time and changed prediction metrics. Here, the matched comparison concerns labelled-session AP, recall and false-positive rates, with exploratory paired-seed intervals for AP differences. Appendix A.4 retains their partition details and uncertainty limitation; their forecasting metrics and network runtime describe a different task and cost boundary.

The present results separate update protection from useful alerting: adding SecAgg+ increased training-workflow time and application-message content, while primary-test mean AP changed only slightly. Relative to the evaluation in Martínez Llamas et al. (2025), the contribution is a matched aggregation comparison with labelled alert outcomes. Their LSTM/Flower/FedAvg application used real hospital logs without anomaly ground truth for detection and false-positive rates. Here, supplied scenario labels support evaluating threats against legitimate exceptions within the benchmark. The studies address related evaluation questions using different data sources.

The measured cost increase belongs to the implemented workflow. Shamim et al. (2026) change the encrypted intrusion-detection stack; Qazi et al. (2026) include component ablations and a headline communication contrast with different round budgets. These interventions differ from adding SecAgg+ to a fixed FedAvg procedure. Overhead therefore depends on the changed components, budget and measurement boundary.

Communication counters also have different boundaries. FeadSeq (Guan et al., 2025) estimates shared-parameter volume for personalised sequence learning on HDFS, BGL, BPIC15 and BPIC20 logs; its examined experiments do not isolate cryptographic SecAgg+. The present counter measures application-message content. Lytvyn and Nguyen (2024) report forecasting quality and training time when adding SecAgg+, supporting joint evaluation of utility and cost. Their task and counted operations differ from session detection and the workflow measured here.

The security interpretation follows the assumptions in Section 2.4 and implementation boundary in Section 3.8. FedAvg (McMahan et al., 2017) and secure aggregation (Bonawitz et al., 2017; Bell et al., 2020; Li et al., 2022) supply the established components. Bell et al.’s proofs and component benchmarks concern specified corruption, dropout and public-key conditions; Li et al. assume authenticated, encrypted links and exclude communication latency from simulation. The local workflows used different diagnostics and no TLS. Their elapsed-time difference measures those workflows; protocol analyses and local checks have distinct evidential roles.

The concentration of false alerts in unusual legitimate activity points to the role of clinical context. Fabbri and LeFevre (2011) used care relationships to explain access, and Hedda et al. (2017) found possible clinical explanations for high-risk rule flags. Those explanations were not independent adjudications of actual misuse. Together with the present error pattern, this work supports assessing whether contextual information helps distinguish legitimate exceptions from threats. That is a model-development question for a new evaluation; neither approach was tested as a modification here.

The false-alert burden also shows why a favourable aggregate metric needs measures of alert quality. Hurst et al. (2022, Table 10) reported test accuracy of 0.9896 with PPV of 0.4486; Table 2.3 retains the validation results and label qualifications. Their density-informed labels and activity units differ from this benchmark. The useful lesson is to report positive-prediction reliability alongside aggregate performance, not to rank these results numerically against the present AP.

Recurring actors and patients in the supplied partitions make performance on new entities a separate question. Menon et al. (2014, Section 4.2) removed raw user and patient identifiers from their Hospital experiment because each user had a constant label, which could reward identity memorisation; cluster identifiers remained. Their relational representation addresses that label-bias problem, but the reported cross-validation does not establish performance on unseen users or patients. Likewise, recurrence in the present data warrants a generalisation question rather than a claim that identity memorisation occurred.

Training only on routine activity leaves legitimate coverage as another concrete development question. Yeng et al. (2021) included normal and nonmalicious abnormal negatives in supervised development; unusual legitimate sessions appeared only in evaluation here. Broader legitimate coverage might reduce false alerts, but this hypothesis remains untested. Senturk et al. (2025) also trained on normal synthetic activity: its vector autoencoder detected 8/12 injected anomalies versus 5/12 for the LSTM, while LSTM false positives fell from three to zero. That operating-point trade-off supports evaluating errors explicitly; it establishes neither a general sequence-modelling advantage nor a direct numerical comparison with session-level AP.

This chapter assesses detection performance across three training approaches and the workflow cost of adding secure aggregation. The approaches are pooled centralised training (A), standard Federated Averaging (FedAvg, B) and FedAvg with Secure Aggregation Plus (SecAgg+, C), implemented using Flower. The method proceeds from source tables and complete sessions through encoding, training, checkpoint selection and validation-based score processing to the two fixed tests.

The design crossed three training approaches, two sampling conditions and five random seeds, producing 30 trained models. A seed fixes the starting point of a run’s random operations. RQ1 compared detection under standard FedAvg and pooled centralised training; RQ2 compared detection and extra workflow cost when SecAgg+ was added to FedAvg. All approaches shared the model architecture, feature encoding, data partitions, loss function, learning rate, batch size, score standardisation, alert-threshold procedure and test sets. Section 3.9 specifies the training budgets. These shared settings supported a controlled computational comparison of training and aggregation procedures.

Following review, the research questions and fourth objective were revised to match the measured comparisons and outcomes. Their revised wording was not fixed before execution. The Evidence Companion retains the original P1 wording.

Routine legitimate sessions were used for training, and routine-only validation supported checkpoint selection, score standardisation and alert-threshold setting. The supplied partitions were retained (Table 3.2). The primary test, test_held_out, contained the held-out threat family low_and_slow_misuse alongside routine and longitudinal_follow_up legitimate sessions. The secondary test, test_known, contained bulk extraction, compromised-account patient hopping, patient snooping and role-action misuse, together with unusual legitimate activity and no routine sessions. Here, held-out refers to the source-designated threat family, and known does not mean that threats were used for training. Appendix C.3 gives the source scenario names and counts. Fixed partitions gave every approach identical evaluation populations; alternative splits were not evaluated.

Two sampling conditions varied how often existing sessions were used for training. Each session was assigned to its most frequent department, with ties resolved by lexical order and no use of threat labels. In each round, Reference sampling randomly ordered every client’s training sessions without replacement. The controlled Non-IID condition used department-skewed sampling with replacement. This label denotes the experimental sampling condition; Reference sampling was not assumed to make clients perfectly independent and identically distributed (IID).

Each client made as many draws as in its own Reference condition. Its designated department received total probability 0.60, and the remaining 0.40 was distributed across other departments in proportion to local session counts. The designated departments were emergency for C1, internal medicine for C2 and surgery for C3. These probabilities were stress settings rather than measured institutional distributions; alternatives were not evaluated. No augmented event sequences were generated: replacement sampling reused existing sessions.

Mean pairwise Jensen–Shannon divergence (JSD), calculated with base-2 logarithms, described differences between department distributions. Checks covered the original distributions, expected department-skewed distributions and observed draws in rounds 1–5 across all five seeds (Tables B.2–B.3). Sampling with replacement also changed the pooled department mix and individual-session frequencies, with possible repeats within a minibatch. The condition therefore combined greater departmental skew with repeated session use; it did not isolate differences between clients as the sole changed factor.

The detector was a compact long short-term memory (LSTM) autoencoder. Its encoder compressed routine access sequences into a shorter representation; its decoder reconstructed their events. New sessions were scored by reconstruction error. Recurrent encoding can represent event order, and reconstruction permits fitting without examples of every threat family (Malhotra et al., 2016). A fixed detector kept the comparison focused on training and aggregation. Appendix B.3 specifies construction order and seed handling; Section 3.9 describes the limits of model and hyperparameter selection.

The encoder processed events in recorded order and compressed each session into a 32-dimensional latent vector, an internal session summary. The model had 86,487 learned parameters. Its single-layer, unidirectional LSTM encoder had 119 input features and a hidden-state size of 64. Initial hidden and cell states were zero. The last valid hidden state passed through a linear projection and hyperbolic tangent (tanh) activation to form the latent vector. Default PyTorch initialisation was retained, with no custom forget-gate bias. The shared 64-unit hidden state and 32-dimensional bottleneck fixed model capacity across training approaches.

The decoder reconstructed each session from its latent vector using an LSTM with input size 32 and hidden-state size 64. The 32-dimensional vector was repeated at each step to the padded batch length. Separate projections initialised hidden and cell states. Decoder inputs excluded ground-truth event vectors, so no teacher forcing was used. To discourage reliance on particular activations during training, dropout omitted decoder-output values with probability 0.10. Separate output layers reconstructed thirteen categorical fields, three Boolean values and six temporal values. Padded positions contributed no loss. Computation used 32-bit floating-point values (float32) on the central processing unit (CPU).

Training minimised a hierarchical reconstruction loss. Categorical fields used cross-entropy, the three Boolean outputs used binary cross-entropy with logits, and the six temporal outputs used Smooth L1 loss (beta = 1.0). Equation (3.1) averages valid targets within each available loss family, then families within an event, events within a session and sessions within a batch.

For each available loss family g, Vᵍᵢₜ is the set of valid targets in family g for event t of session i, and Gᵢₜ contains the families with at least one valid target. Boolean and temporal sets contain three and six outputs, respectively; the categorical set contains the valid fields among thirteen. Tᵢ is the valid session length, and B is the batch of sessions. Padding is excluded. When no categorical targets are valid, Gᵢₜ contains only Boolean and temporal families, so each receives half the event weight. Otherwise each family receives one third. Batch loss averages the session scores sᵢ, giving each session equal weight regardless of length. All approaches used this rule; alternatives were not compared.

For illustration only, family losses 0.3, 0.3 and 0.6 give event loss 0.4. With no valid categorical targets, Boolean and temporal losses 0.2 and 0.4 give event loss 0.3. An illustrative session with event losses 0.4, 0.3, 0.3, 0.3 and 0.3 has raw score 0.32 and exceeds an illustrative raw threshold of 0.30. These values explain the arithmetic; they are not benchmark observations.

A session’s raw anomaly score was its mean reconstruction loss across valid events. Higher reconstruction loss was treated as more anomalous. This score direction was not reversed after examining test results. Scoring used eval() and no_grad() to disable training behaviour and gradient calculation, with checks that parameters remained unchanged.

For pooled ranking metrics, each client’s raw session losses were robustly standardised using that client’s routine-validation scores from the checkpoint selected by routine-validation loss. Scores were transformed as z = (loss − median)/scale, with scale = 1.482602218505602 × MAD; MAD is the median absolute deviation from the median. A scale at most 1e-12 was replaced by IQR/1.3489795003921634, where IQR is the difference between the 75th and 25th percentiles. If this was also at most 1e-12, scale became 1.0. Records identified the scaling method and any unit-scale fallback. The transformed scores aligned client scales for pooled AP and AUROC; they did not estimate threat probabilities. A positive affine mapping preserves ranking within each client, but client-specific transformations can change the pooled ranking. Alert decisions used raw losses as described below.

Each client’s alert rule compared raw session loss with a client-specific routine-validation quantile, calculated by linear interpolation. The primary threshold was the 99th percentile, the upper 1% boundary of that validation distribution. The 98th and 99.5th percentiles were retained for prespecified sensitivity analyses. An alert required a raw score strictly greater than the client’s threshold. Records linked the thresholds and score-standardisation parameters to the selected model and validation scores. These upper-tail settings used no threat labels and were procedural choices rather than a clinically validated alert budget.

Using the same routine-validation sessions for checkpoint selection, score standardisation and threshold setting may make their assessment appear more favourable. The 99th-percentile threshold is based on that sample; its false-positive rate on a separate test depends on the test-score distribution and is not fixed at 1%. Test results were not used to adjust thresholds.

Flower coordinated federated training through a server application (ServerApp) and three client applications. One SuperLink coordinated three SuperNodes connecting the ClientApps, and communication used the research computer’s loopback interface. Each ClientApp loaded its assigned sequence files. Process and application identities were checked before execution; Section 3.1 defines the shared-host administration and data-access boundary.

The experiments used the research-local Flower build 1.22.0+mai.prg7570.1 with a counter-based HMAC-SHA256 masking helper adapted from a fixed contributor revision (saurabhvmagdum, 2026). Appendix B.5 records the backport and validation history. The exact historical installed package was unavailable; Section 4.11 distinguishes candidate-package and retained-file checks from verification of that installation.

Before the accepted main experiments, predefined public-vector tests checked secure-aggregation averages with equal and unequal weights, numerical rounding and conditions requiring refusal. Table B.1 and Table B.4 give expected aggregates, errors and acceptance limits, including the main-run client weights. Appendix B.5 explains the numerical-range choices; they were not selected through privacy-leakage optimisation.

The clipping_range setting of 8.0 defined the configured numerical range. Project input checks rejected non-finite parameters and unweighted values with absolute magnitude above 8, rather than accepting those out-of-range values through clipping. Protection covered individual model updates during aggregation; the aggregate, shared models, metrics, counts, plaintext preprocessing summaries and researcher-side score processing remained outside that protection. Information leakage from EHR updates, the aggregate or final model was not quantified.

After the main benchmark and computational replay, seven groups of local implementation checks ran in the retained Flower 1.22.0+mai.prg7570.1 environment. Acceptance criteria and script identities were fixed before those checks, when benchmark results were already known. Public arrays and single-round computations exercised installed Flower code and selected project validators, without EHR training or inference. Appendix B.5 gives the checks’ design and counting history, and Appendix C.7 documents the cases and controls. Their scope did not cover the complete application or a network deployment.

A separately versioned project patch made the collection-request validator reject inconsistent peer lists before the affected client’s local computation. Retesting used the original acceptance criteria and public inputs; the installed cryptographic helper was unchanged. Appendix B.5 describes the rule and retest design, and Appendix C.7 retains the original failure, correction and distinct test ledgers.

Five fixed seeds, 11, 29, 47, 71 and 97, assessed variation from training randomness. Matched approaches reused initial model states and sampling schedules saved before the main experiments. Table 3.6 gives the common loss, learning rate, batch size and other settings; optimiser-state lifetime and update order differed between pooled and federated training (Section 3.6). The files contain no documented comparison of LSTM with other model families or comparative search explaining the adopted hidden sizes, latent sizes, dropout rate, learning rate, batch size or budget. No additional seed, hyperparameter or post-test architecture search was conducted. Thirty epochs or rounds fixed how often sessions were scheduled for training without guaranteeing convergence.

Pre-main-run engineering checks exercised preprocessing, learning, aggregation, timing and inference on routine training and validation partitions, without test data and with a shorter training budget. Appendix B.5 separates these engineering runs and their corrections from the accepted main experiments; excluded earlier blocks and fixed-input reruns remain documented.

Evaluation assessed score ranking and threat identification through alerts. Threat sessions were positive; routine and unusual legitimate sessions were negative. The primary measure, average precision (AP), summarises how well threats rank near the top. It relates threat ranking to the precision attained as recall changes, making it relevant to prioritising possible threats for review. AP also depends on class proportions, so the two test populations must be interpreted separately. The supporting measure, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), measures how often threats score above legitimate sessions. Global AP and AUROC used scores pooled after client-wise standardisation with routine-validation data (Section 3.5.2). Raw scores were used for secondary global results and client-level measures. Worst-client AP was the minimum of three client AP values for each model run and test set; the client identity was retained. AP meant average precision, not trapezoidal area under the precision–recall curve. Each test retained its original class proportions (Table 3.7).

Paired differences compared approaches using the same seed, shared initial state and sampling schedule. Exploratory 95% intervals for mean differences in global and worst-client AP used mean(d) ± t(0.975, 4) × SD(d)/√5. Here, d contains five within-seed differences for one comparison, and SD(d) is their sample standard deviation. The value t(0.975, 4) is the 97.5th percentile of Student’s t distribution with four degrees of freedom. The exploratory calculation required five finite matched pairs. As a reporting rule, intervals were omitted when the paired differences had zero variance. They describe training-seed variability on the fixed benchmark, not variation between independent hospitals or clinical populations.

The group diagnostics split the session score in Equation (3.1) into additive categorical, Boolean and temporal contributions using the same valid-target, family and event denominators. Their sum reconstructs the adopted anomaly score. Two calculations kept model outputs unchanged and varied only the score arithmetic: one used thirteen as the categorical denominator; the other omitted ward_or_location’s output term and renormalised the remaining categorical terms. Neither calculation removed an input, retrained the model or produced a newly calibrated detector. Component shares and descriptive associations show how the score is composed, rather than the causal importance of inputs.

The replay repeated 30 centralised epochs or federated rounds, with checkpoints and validation-only score processing fixed before scoring both tests. Full-precision comparisons covered initial and selected tensor states, selected rounds, validation scores, score standardisation, thresholds, test scores, metrics and paired-seed summaries. Appendix C.6 explains the historical scaler-JSON compatibility view; fresh raw preprocessing outputs were preserved. This was a rebuilt Python environment on the same host, without reconstruction of the complete historical operating-system image. Section 4.10 reports the outcomes, and the Evidence Companion retains execution and compatibility records.

Appendix C.8 documents code, data and artifact availability and indexes the local evidence supplement, including result derivations, computational-replay records, bounded security checks and supplementary analysis code. Complete experiment source, the raw benchmark, learned weights and the offline dependency store remain in the author-held environment and are excluded from the supplement. Dataset access and redistribution rights require clarification before external sharing; no verified public release is claimed.

Federated learning trains a shared model without pooling raw electronic health record (EHR) access logs, but the server can still inspect individual model updates. This study compared detection performance and workflow cost with and without secure aggregation. Pooled centralised training, standard Federated Averaging and Federated Averaging with Secure Aggregation Plus (SecAgg+) used the same long short-term memory (LSTM) autoencoder to reconstruct routine access sessions. Experiments used one supplied benchmark described as synthetic, three simulated clients and five random seeds. Reference sampling retained the original client distributions; controlled Non-IID sampling favoured selected departments through resampling. On the primary test, which included threats, routine access and unusual legitimate activity, SecAgg+ achieved mean global average precision (AP) of 0.421 and 0.429, respectively. Mean paired AP differences, calculated as SecAgg+ minus standard Federated Averaging, were +0.0047 and +0.0001. These estimates did not establish equivalent performance. Federated training did not consistently outperform pooled training. Relative to standard Federated Averaging, SecAgg+ increased recorded training-workflow time by 132.8% and 128.6%, and application-message content by approximately 49.9%. All configurations struggled with unusual legitimate activity. SecAgg+ had mean false-positive rates of 98.58% and 96.40% on the secondary test, which contained threats and unusual legitimate activity without routine sessions. A fresh-environment replay on the same computer reproduced the predictions, with a disclosed input-scaling metadata exception. The comparison quantifies the workflow cost of masking updates and identifies persistent false alerts on legitimate exceptions. Protection depended on a trusted host and honest participants. Incomplete data-generation records and simulated clients limit implications for hospitals.
Keywords: EHR access anomaly detection, federated learning, LSTM autoencoder, Flower, Secure Aggregation Plus (SecAgg+).

Pembelajaran bersekutu melatih model bersama tanpa memusatkan log capaian rekod kesihatan elektronik (EHR), tetapi pelayan masih boleh memeriksa kemas kini model individu. Kajian ini membandingkan prestasi pengesanan dan kos aliran kerja dengan dan tanpa pengagregatan selamat. Latihan berpusat terkumpul, Federated Averaging standard dan Federated Averaging dengan Secure Aggregation Plus (SecAgg+) menggunakan autoenkoder long short-term memory (LSTM) yang sama untuk membina semula sesi capaian rutin. Eksperimen menggunakan satu penanda aras yang dibekalkan dan dihuraikan sebagai sintetik, tiga klien simulasi dan lima seed rawak. Pensampelan Reference mengekalkan taburan klien asal; pensampelan Non-IID terkawal mengutamakan jabatan terpilih melalui pensampelan semula. Dalam ujian utama yang merangkumi ancaman serta aktiviti sah rutin dan luar biasa, SecAgg+ mencapai min average precision (AP) global sebanyak 0.421 dan 0.429, masing-masing. Perbezaan min AP berpasangan, yang dikira sebagai AP SecAgg+ tolak AP Federated Averaging standard, ialah +0.0047 dan +0.0001. Anggaran ini tidak membuktikan kesetaraan prestasi. Latihan bersekutu tidak secara konsisten mengatasi latihan berpusat terkumpul. Berbanding Federated Averaging standard, SecAgg+ meningkatkan masa aliran kerja latihan yang direkodkan sebanyak 132.8% dan 128.6%, serta kandungan mesej aplikasi kira-kira 49.9%. Semua konfigurasi sukar membezakan ancaman daripada aktiviti sah yang luar biasa. Min kadar positif palsu SecAgg+ ialah 98.58% dan 96.40% dalam ujian sekunder yang mengandungi ancaman dan aktiviti sah luar biasa tanpa sesi rutin. Pengulangan dalam persekitaran perisian baharu pada komputer yang sama menghasilkan semula ramalan, dengan pengecualian metadata penskalaan input yang didokumenkan. Perbandingan ini mengukur kos aliran kerja untuk menyamarkan kemas kini dan mengenal pasti masalah berterusan berupa amaran palsu terhadap aktiviti sah luar biasa. Perlindungan bergantung pada hos yang dipercayai dan peserta yang jujur. Rekod penjanaan data yang tidak lengkap dan klien simulasi mengehadkan implikasi dapatan untuk hospital.
Kata kunci: pengesanan anomali akses EHR, pembelajaran bersekutu, autoenkoder LSTM, Flower, Secure Aggregation Plus (SecAgg+).

Electronic health records (EHRs) store patient information; audit logs record who accessed it. Monitoring logs can help investigators examine potentially inappropriate access. Unusual patterns alone do not establish misuse because clinical duties and exceptional work may explain them (Fabbri & LeFevre, 2011; Hedda et al., 2017). Collaborative monitoring therefore requires evidence about both training without pooling sensitive activity records and distinguishing threats from legitimate exceptions. This study evaluates these requirements through matched training comparisons on a project-supplied benchmark.

Keeping records at clients does not make updates private. Depending on the model and training conditions, an update may reveal information about its training data (Hatamizadeh et al., 2023). Standard FedAvg exposes each client’s update separately to the server. Secure Aggregation lets the server obtain the combined update without directly inspecting individual contributions during aggregation, provided the protocol’s assumptions hold (Bonawitz et al., 2017).

Detection quality, update protection and workflow cost need to be assessed together. Protecting updates can add coordination and computation without making alerts more meaningful. Repeated alerts on legitimate emergency or reassignment activity would still require careful human investigation. The evaluation therefore measures protected-aggregation cost and separately examines errors on routine and unusual legitimate sessions.

The task uses EHR access sequences because patterns across events may be harder to see in individual log entries (Rule et al., 2020). A session is a sequence of accesses grouped in the supplied dataset. The detector is a long short-term memory (LSTM) autoencoder that processes ordered events and is trained to reconstruct routine sessions. Reconstruction error measures the difference between original and reconstructed inputs; larger errors receive higher anomaly scores.

Unusual activity may still be legitimate when clinical context explains it (Fabbri & LeFevre, 2011; Hedda et al., 2017). The benchmark labels emergency work, staff reassignment and high-volume auditing or reporting as legitimate (Appendix C.3). Evaluation must distinguish threats from both routine and unusual legitimate activity.

The experiment compares pooled centralised training, standard Flower FedAvg and Flower FedAvg with Secure Aggregation Plus (SecAgg+). Pooled training combines records; standard FedAvg trains at clients; SecAgg+ masks client contributions during aggregation. Detection results are assessed alongside training-workflow time and application-message content. The three clients are simulated on one trusted research computer; Section 3.10 defines the measurement boundaries.

The closest EHR application combined an LSTM autoencoder, Flower and FedAvg but lacked anomaly ground truth for estimating detection and false-positive rates (Martínez Llamas et al., 2025). A matched evaluation is therefore needed to examine detection outcomes alongside the cost of masking client updates. The present study holds the detector, sampling schedules and evaluation procedure constant when comparing standard FedAvg with FedAvg with SecAgg+. Update protection and alert quality remain distinct outcomes: masking limits direct inspection during aggregation, while source-labelled tests assess threat ranking and alert errors.

The evaluation first compares standard FedAvg with pooled centralised training, then compares standard FedAvg with FedAvg with SecAgg+. Pooled training supplies a performance reference for these benchmark comparisons.

This study aims to evaluate detection quality and the workflow cost of protecting individual client updates in a federated EHR anomaly detector. It compares pooled and federated training, then standard FedAvg and FedAvg with SecAgg+, using recorded training-workflow time and application-message content alongside detection measures.

The study provides a matched empirical comparison of federated EHR anomaly-detection workflows with and without SecAgg+, with pooled centralised training as a performance reference. The federated workflows share an LSTM-autoencoder architecture, sampling schedules and evaluation procedure, allowing detection differences to be examined alongside the measured cost of protecting updates. This is an empirical and implementation contribution using established model and software components.

The comparison quantifies added workflow time and application-message content, identifies persistent false alerts on unusual legitimate activity, and documents same-host computational reproduction within the limits in Sections 4.10 and 5.7. These findings separate three questions for EHR monitoring: whether updates are masked, what that workflow costs, and whether its alerts distinguish threats from legitimate exceptions.

Across the matched runs, adding SecAgg+ increased training-workflow time and application-message content, while mean AP differences from standard FedAvg were small. All three methods frequently flagged unusual legitimate activity. The chapter reports detection and cost comparisons, explains the errors by legitimate behaviour, and presents reproduction, security checks and post-test diagnostics. The Evidence Companion contains individual-run results.

All ten matched experimental blocks completed, producing 30 trained models (Table 4.1). On the shared research host, standard FedAvg exchanged trained parameters and FedAvg with SecAgg+ exchanged masked contributions; neither sent raw event records. Section 3.7 describes these simulated exchanges.

Training completed 153,600 optimiser steps across the three methods and 600 aggregation operations across the two federated methods. FedAvg with SecAgg+ completed 1,200 protocol stages, with all three clients participating throughout and no fallback to ordinary FedAvg.

Department-biased resampling increased mean pairwise departmental Jensen–Shannon divergence from 0.003765 bits in the original distributions to an expected 0.330615 bits. Across five seeds, observed values in rounds 1–5 ranged from 0.330714 to 0.334338 bits (Tables B.2–B.3, which retain department proportions). These selected-round checks describe the intended shift in department mix; resampling also changed session frequencies and did not isolate heterogeneity alone.

Public-vector checks supported numerical agreement and rejection of the tested incomplete requests. With main-run client counts as weights, the recorded error was 1.474 × 10⁻⁶, below the 1.056 × 10⁻⁵ limit; missing replies or mismatched identifiers prevented aggregation calls (Tables B.1 and B.4). Section 4.11 reports the later local checks.

The primary held-out test contained one gradual-misuse threat scenario (low_and_slow_misuse). Legitimate activity comprised routine sessions and longitudinal follow-up (longitudinal_follow_up). Each client had 63 threat sessions; clients C1, C2 and C3 had 721, 743 and 711 legitimate sessions. The secondary known-scenario test contained four threat families and unusual legitimate activity, with no routine sessions. Appendix C.3 gives scenario labels and counts. These supplied scenario labels do not represent independently confirmed hospital incidents.

The partitions shared no session IDs, and their recorded UTC time ranges were chronologically ordered and non-overlapping. Actor and patient IDs recurred across partitions. The original partitioning algorithm was unavailable, and the absence of individual-device identifiers prevented assessment of device overlap. Post-test client-level checks found that every evaluated session used actors already present in that client’s training data (Section 4.12; Table C.10).

All held-out threat and longitudinal-follow-up sessions contained exactly five events. Routine sessions contained 6–23 events, with a mean of 9.93. No experiment isolated the effects of session length or recurring actors and patients on detection performance.

Global AP and AUROC used scores placed on a comparable scale with each client’s routine-validation data; client-level metrics used raw reconstruction loss. Alerts required a raw score above the client’s 99th-percentile validation threshold (q = 0.99). The primary threshold remained fixed after testing, and the higher-loss score direction was not reversed. Section 3.10 defines the measures.

Threat sessions were positive cases; routine and unusual legitimate sessions were negative cases, with their original proportions retained. The evaluation therefore tests threat discrimination against legitimate activity, rather than unusualness alone.

Stored-score recalculation reproduced ranking and alert-decision metrics. Separate checks recovered calibration, model selection and federated cost records; same-host retraining and inference provided the computational reproduction evidence in Section 4.10.

The ranking advantage depended on the sampling condition. Mean global AP favoured pooled centralised training under Reference sampling and standard FedAvg under controlled Non-IID sampling (Table 4.4). FedAvg with SecAgg+ achieved AP of 0.4208 and 0.4294, respectively. Giving every test session the same score would yield AP = 189/2,364 ≈ 0.07995, the threat proportion. Primary-test paired AP differences were −0.0697 and +0.0238 for standard FedAvg minus pooled training, and +0.0047 and +0.0001 for SecAgg+ minus standard FedAvg. All four exploratory 95% intervals included zero (Table 4.9).

High overall AUROC must be read alongside the legitimate subgroups. For FedAvg with SecAgg+ under Reference sampling, overall AUROC was 0.9437, but subgroup AUROC was 0.9925 against routine sessions and 0.4307 against legitimate follow-up. Routine sessions made up 91.31% of the negatives, so their strong separation dominated the overall value. Section 4.8.2 gives the negative-count-weighted decomposition.

The post-test length-only diagnostic also identified a cue in this test’s composition: ranking shorter sessions first gave AUROC 0.95655 (Section 4.12). Both threats and legitimate follow-up contained five events, whereas routine sessions contained at least six. This descriptive ranking neither validates a replacement detector nor establishes that the LSTM relied on length.

Figure 4.3 shows AP variation across five training seeds on the same fixed test. Under Reference sampling, pooled training varied more (SD = 0.1175) than standard FedAvg (0.0491) or FedAvg with SecAgg+ (0.0536). Across the six method–sampling combinations, mean overall AUROC ranged from 0.9430 to 0.9537.

At the fixed alert thresholds, FedAvg with SecAgg+ detected most labelled threats, but only approximately half or fewer of its alerts corresponded to threats. Mean recall was 84.97% under Reference sampling and 82.01% under controlled Non-IID sampling; corresponding precision was 46.00% and 49.85% (Table 4.5). These decisions used each client’s primary validation threshold, q = 0.99.

The secondary scenario test showed poor separation of threats from unusual legitimate activity. It contained 378 threat sessions and 267 unusual legitimate sessions, with no routine activity; the detector had been trained only on routine legitimate sessions. Giving all sessions the same score would yield AP = 378/645 ≈ 0.58605. FedAvg with SecAgg+ had lower mean AP: 0.4040 under Reference sampling and 0.4113 under controlled Non-IID sampling. Its mean AUROC was also below 0.5, at 0.1432 and 0.1692, respectively (Table 4.6). Similar AP values across the test sets therefore have different meanings relative to their constant-score references.

Client-level results show whether pooled performance conceals a weak participant result (Table 4.8). Worst-client AP was the minimum of the three client values within each method, sampling condition and seed; the reported mean and sample SD summarise these five minima. Appendix C.4 lists every client value and tied minimum. On the primary test, C1 had higher mean AP than C2 for both federated methods and sampling conditions. These descriptive differences do not explain the causes of client variation.

Table 4.9 brings together AP contrasts paired by seed, sampling condition and test set. B−A denotes standard FedAvg minus pooled centralised training. The primary-test differences, −0.0697 under Reference sampling and +0.0238 under controlled Non-IID sampling, changed direction and had exploratory 95% intervals spanning zero. Thus, standard FedAvg did not consistently rank above pooled training across the two conditions.

The post-test false-alert breakdown uses the original q = 0.99 decisions from FedAvg with SecAgg+ to compare routine and unusual legitimate activity (Table 4.10; Figure 4.5). Each legitimate group’s session count is its FPR denominator. Single-class groups have error rates and counts, without AP or AUROC; Appendix C.4 indexes per-seed results for all three methods.

The weights reflect the negative groups’ sizes, rather than the common number of threats; unusual legitimate activity here is longitudinal follow-up.

Most unusual legitimate sessions remained flagged at q = 0.995 despite the loss of threat recall. This prespecified sensitivity analysis changed only the threshold, retaining stored scores and rankings; q = 0.99 remained primary, without additional threshold search or score reversal.

Only purpose_of_use and relationship_type had excluded categorical targets in either test; the other eleven fields had none (Table 4.12). Under the rule shared by every method and seed, missing values and categories absent from training were excluded as targets. Exclusion percentages use thirteen possible targets per real, non-padding event as their denominator. This coverage check provides context for the fixed-output representation diagnostics in Section 4.12.

A fresh-environment replay on the same host reproduced the compared predictive outputs across 30 training runs and 60 model–test evaluations. Initial and selected tensors, selected rounds, validation scores, calibration, raw and calibrated test scores, metrics and paired-seed summaries matched the historical reference. All 90,270 score rows and alert decisions at q = 0.98, 0.99 and 0.995 agreed. The rows repeatedly evaluate 3,009 distinct sessions, not independent observations.

One scaler diagnostic differed by one adjacent float64 value, although applied scaling parameters and all 30 regenerated arrays matched. A compatibility file set reused the historical scaler JSON with the regenerated arrays to satisfy the original scaler-file hash (Appendix C.6). Predictions and numerical inputs therefore matched without identical preprocessing-metadata bytes.

Export checks distinguished model payloads from diagnostic metadata. Nine selected SV-07 payload-safe outputs contained none of nine public test canaries, whereas the deliberately unsafe control contained all nine. Two artifacts nevertheless retained a public marker in permitted diagnostic fields: request IDs, exception-class names and traceback file or function information. Payload-safe names a test category, not a general release guarantee: permitted metadata still requires review for arbitrary or sensitive content before external sharing (Appendix C.7).

Post-test diagnostics examined test composition and existing scores using the fixed supplied data and all 30 selected checkpoints. They covered length, recurring actors and patients, categorical-target coverage, duplicated location fields and loss contributions. Models, representations and thresholds were unchanged. New inference exactly reproduced all 90,270 original raw scores across 60 model–test evaluations; additive contributions reconstructed each score within 9.54 × 10⁻⁷ because of float32 summation order, with zero difference for the original-score comparison.

Loss decomposition describes each reconstruction group’s contribution to existing scores (Table 4.18). In FedAvg with SecAgg+, Boolean reconstruction contributed 81.32–81.69% of mean held-out threat scores and 84.66–87.05% of mean held-out unusual-legitimate scores across the two conditions, compared with 2.06–2.26% for routine activity. In the known test, its share was 68.82–69.48% for unusual legitimate activity and 23.34–24.95% for threats. The similar Boolean dominance in the two held-out nonroutine classes accompanies their weak score separation and high false-alert rates (Section 4.8). These additive shares describe the adopted loss, rather than causal input importance or a retrained ablation.

Department and ward_or_location values matched in all 181,805 logged events, supplying duplicate recorded information. The fixed-output calculations examined this representation without changing model inputs, predictions, calibration or performance results.

Dividing summed valid categorical-field losses by thirteen, instead of the valid-field count, reduced FedAvg with SecAgg+’s mean class-level raw scores by approximately 0.15–1.57%. Omitting only the ward_or_location output term and renormalising the remaining terms increased those means by approximately 0.39–5.77%, because that output had relatively low reconstruction error. These calculations do not establish the effect of removing duplicated inputs and retraining. Causal explanations require controlled representation studies with fresh evaluation.

Global AP favoured pooled centralised training or standard FedAvg depending on sampling, without a consistent federated advantage. Adding SecAgg+ changed primary-test mean paired AP by +0.0047 under Reference sampling and +0.0001 under controlled Non-IID sampling; exploratory intervals included zero. The principal detection weakness was unusual legitimate activity: its secondary-test mean FPR for FedAvg with SecAgg+ was 98.58% and 96.40%, respectively (Sections 4.4–4.8).

Same-host replay reproduced the compared predictive outputs across 30 runs and 60 model–test evaluations, subject to the scaler-metadata exception and differing resource measurements. Local security checks identified an input-rejection defect, verified a targeted correction and exposed a permitted-metadata release limitation. Sections 4.10–4.11 give the separate evidence and scope of these checks.

Protected federated training exchanged masked client updates at a measurable workflow cost. On the shared research host, FedAvg with SecAgg+ took longer and carried more application-message content than standard FedAvg, while mean paired primary-test AP differences were small (Tables 4.9 and 4.14). Unusual legitimate activity still triggered frequent false alerts. The comparison therefore separates the cost of the implemented protected workflow from the unresolved usefulness of alerts and the operating budget needed to judge cost acceptability.

The RQ1 comparison changed direction with sampling. Primary-test mean global AP favoured pooled centralised training under Reference sampling and standard FedAvg under controlled Non-IID sampling; both exploratory 95% intervals for paired differences included zero. Pooled training had higher mean AP in both conditions on the secondary test (Table 4.9). Thus, the tested federated workflow offered no consistent global-AP advantage across conditions and tests.

Federated training exchanged parameters without sending raw session records to the aggregation server. All processes nevertheless shared a host on which the researcher could access client files (Section 3.8), so the comparison represents simulated collaboration with shared administration.

Resampling changed session frequencies in both pooled and client training data. Together with different parameter-update sequences, this prevents attributing the changed AP ordering to heterogeneity alone (Section 3.6). No local-only models were compared, so the evaluation also leaves collaboration’s benefit over independent client training unresolved.

The federated workflows showed small observed detection differences. Mean paired primary-test global AP differences for FedAvg with SecAgg+ minus standard FedAvg were +0.0047 under Reference sampling and +0.0001 under controlled Non-IID sampling. Both exploratory 95% intervals included zero (Table 4.9), without establishing equivalence.

Quantisation may affect later optimisation, but its effect was not isolated from the masking helper, diagnostic checks or other implementation details. The estimates therefore compare complete workflows. No validated margin for acceptable detection loss was specified for an intended application, leaving practical acceptability unresolved.

These costs describe a workflow without Transport Layer Security (TLS), which protects data in transit; SecAgg+ combined with TLS was not evaluated. Section 5.7.5 consolidates the aggregation boundary and visible outputs. Table 5.1 summarises the findings supported by this comparison.

Overall AUROC obscured the legitimate-exception problem because routine sessions comprised 91.31% of primary-test negatives. Strong separation from that large routine group yielded AUROC near 0.94 despite weak separation from legitimate follow-up (Section 4.8.2). AUROC summarises ordering across thresholds, whereas FPR describes false alerts at the chosen threshold. On the secondary test, protected-model AP of 0.4040 and 0.4113 was below the constant-score reference of 0.58605 in both conditions (Section 4.5). The negative comparison group therefore changes the meaning of an apparently similar AP value.

The secondary-test scores tended to rank unusual legitimate activity above threats under the supplied labels. This weakness occurred in raw and calibrated pooled scores and raw within-client scores (Section 4.6), so calibration alone cannot explain it. Routine-only training, incomplete context and synthetic-data construction are possible explanations whose separate effects were not established. The source labels were not independently assessed for clinical validity (Section 5.7.1).

Ranking by length alone gave high overall held-out AUROC but could not separate the two five-event nonroutine classes (Table 4.17). This post-test descriptor shows why pooled ranking should also be examined within legitimate subgroups.

Boolean reconstruction contributed substantially to protected-model scores for held-out threats and unusual legitimate activity (Table 4.18). Anonymous examples include a legitimate session with a high Boolean contribution and a threat with a much smaller one (Table C.12). These fixed-score patterns do not establish whether deleting an input would improve detection.

The study provides a working federated EHR anomaly-detection workflow and a matched comparison of update masking, detection and workflow cost. Standard FedAvg and FedAvg with SecAgg+ used the same architecture, sampling schedules and calibration procedure. The resulting evidence quantifies protection cost, exposes errors on legitimate exceptions and documents computational reproduction on the existing host. These are implementation and empirical contributions using established components; Section 6.3 links them to the study objectives.

False alerts are the main obstacle to practical use. In the primary test, FedAvg with SecAgg+ had mean precision of approximately 46–50% and about 72–87 false alerts per 1,000 legitimate sessions across the two sampling conditions. The secondary test used a different legitimate denominator: only unusual legitimate activity, which all three methods frequently flagged (Table 4.7). These benchmark rates describe alert selectivity, not an estimated hospital review workload.

Responsible institutional evaluation would require access controls, authenticated transport, appropriate retention and export review around the SecAgg+ workflow. Those controls were not validated as a complete patient and employee privacy framework. Section 5.7.5 consolidates the outputs and actors outside the tested protection boundary.

The study did not measure fairness or compare alert burdens across departments, roles or demographic groups. Client-level results are not a fairness assessment. Future evaluation should examine disproportionate flagging of legitimate activity in defined groups, using adequate denominators and contextual review.

The common detector, inputs, partitions, training hyperparameters, calibration and test sets reduced alternative explanations for performance differences. Training procedures still differed: AdamW state was reset at each centralised epoch or client fit, with different update sequences. Department-biased resampling changed session frequencies in pooled and client data. Timing also includes diagnostic checks that differed between standard FedAvg and FedAvg with SecAgg+ (Section 3.6).

Dataset provenance, use and redistribution rights, and formal ethics status remain unverified (Sections 3.2 and 3.12; Appendix C.1). The creator and generation process were not established by authentic records. Resolving these unknowns requires source documentation and the responsible institution’s determination. File hashes identify the analysed snapshot; successful replay establishes repeatable execution. Neither establishes data origin, permitted use or ethics approval.

The local tests support selected masking-helper, message-check and numerical-aggregation behaviours. They found no reuse among the compared key and mask contexts, and a targeted SV-05 retest verified a correction without repeating the complete historical suite. The aggregate, shared models, scalar outputs including metrics, plaintext preprocessing summaries, researcher-side calibration and local files remained outside aggregation protection. Permitted diagnostic metadata still assumes public, trusted contents; the researcher could access client files on the shared host. These checks neither measured leakage nor established cryptographic certification, arbitrary-collusion resistance, host-administrator isolation or TLS protection (Section 4.11; Appendix C.7).

Predictive outputs matched, but preprocessing metadata had one exception. Applied scaling parameters and encoded arrays matched, while one scaler diagnostic differed by one float64 step; matching the required file identity used the compatibility binding in Appendix C.6. The replay therefore reproduced compared predictive outputs rather than every preprocessing byte or intermediate training trajectory. Resource timings and SecAgg+ message content also differed without a controlled explanation. External-host replication and reconstruction from the original generator remain unverified.

Table 5.2 links each limitation to follow-up evidence. Priorities are authentic data-provenance, permission and ethics records, followed by representative legitimate cases and independently reviewed labels. These inputs are needed to connect detection estimates to appropriate and inappropriate access in the intended setting. Work informed by observed test results must be identified as post-test; revised models, representations or thresholds require fresh evaluation.

Retrospective evaluation used complete sessions from one supplied benchmark described as synthetic. Three methods, two sampling conditions and five seeds produced 30 selected models and 60 model–test evaluations, with routine-validation calibration fixed before testing. The clients shared one trusted research host, defining the simulated setting of these findings.

For RQ1, the global-AP comparison changed direction with sampling. Standard FedAvg minus pooled centralised training gave mean paired differences of −0.0697 under Reference sampling and +0.0238 under controlled Non-IID sampling, with both exploratory 95% intervals including zero (Tables 4.4, 4.6 and 4.9). Under controlled Non-IID sampling, higher FedAvg AP accompanied lower recall and F1 at q = 0.99 (Tables 4.4 and 4.5). All three methods frequently flagged unusual legitimate secondary-test sessions (Table 4.7).

Thus, federated training did not consistently improve global AP over pooled training in this benchmark. The evaluation compared these training organisations; independent local-only models would be needed to assess the benefit of collaboration over client-only training.

For RQ2, adding SecAgg+ changed primary-test mean paired global AP by +0.0047 under Reference sampling and +0.0001 under controlled Non-IID sampling. Both exploratory 95% intervals included zero, without establishing equivalence (Table 4.9). Mean paired recorded training-workflow time increased by 132.78% and 128.64%, respectively; application-message content increased by approximately 49.90% (Tables 4.13–4.14). The counter excludes network framing, retransmissions and infrastructure traffic.

The added time covered whole workflows with differing diagnostic checks, rather than isolated cryptographic computation (Section 4.9.1). SecAgg+ masked individual updates under the stated assumptions; leakage was not measured, and cost acceptability requires an operational budget.

The study provides a matched empirical comparison of federated EHR anomaly-detection workflows with and without SecAgg+. It measures detection outcomes alongside workflow cost and examines false alerts on unusual legitimate activity. The working implementation combines an established LSTM-autoencoder family, Flower and an attributed helper backport. Table 6.1 links the four objectives in Section 1.4 to the implementation and empirical evidence.

The comparison identified persistent errors on legitimate exceptions. On the secondary known-scenario test, mean FPR for FedAvg with SecAgg+ was 98.58% under Reference sampling and 96.40% under controlled Non-IID sampling (Table 4.7). Masking updates therefore left a substantial detection problem in the tested model and benchmark. These errors must be considered alongside the small AP differences and added workflow cost when assessing a future application.

The evaluation makes ranking, alert decisions and legitimate subgroups separately visible. Supplementary diagnostics identified a class-related length cue and described reconstruction-loss contributions, without isolating causal input effects (Section 4.12).

A fresh-environment replay on the existing host reproduced the compared predictive results and selected tensor states (Section 4.10; Appendix C.6). Its evidence is computational reproducibility on the fixed snapshot, subject to the scaler-metadata exception and different resource measurements; it is not independent detection validation. Generalisation beyond the benchmark remains unresolved.

Local security checks identified a rejection defect and verified a targeted correction; the full original failure and retest remain documented in Section 4.11 and Appendix C.7. Permitted diagnostic metadata still requires release review. The checks did not quantify privacy leakage, establish comprehensive replay-attack resistance or isolate client files from the shared-host administrator.

The immediate priorities are authentic data-origin records and representative examples of unusual legitimate activity. Table 5.2 specifies the supporting studies and evidence needed. Any revised model, representation or threshold should receive fresh evaluation reported separately from the completed fixed-benchmark comparison.

The implemented SecAgg+ workflow masked individual updates under the stated assumptions, at higher training-workflow cost and with persistent false alerts on legitimate exceptions. The study’s central finding is that update confidentiality, workflow cost and alert quality require separate evidence in federated EHR monitoring. Its matched measurements and error analysis provide that distinction for this benchmark and a basis for the controlled application studies in Table 5.2.

An audit log shows what a user accessed, but may not explain why it was clinically appropriate (Rule et al., 2020). Access monitoring therefore needs clinical context to distinguish suspicious activity from legitimate work that happens to be unusual.

Privacy-officer labels and independently identified incidents support different evaluation claims. Boxwala et al. (2011) used logistic regression and support vector machines (SVMs) on accesses labelled suspicious or appropriate. Kim et al. (2011) selected logistic-regression examples through anomaly and signature filters, combining filter-selected positives with control-sample negatives. Their separate incident tests contained only positive cases: independently investigated accesses for Boxwala et al. and independently identified accesses for Kim et al. These tests estimated sensitivity, but not an independent false-positive rate. Table 2.3 gives sample sizes and results; Appendix A.4 retains the training-sample selection details.

Relational approaches interpret access through relationships among staff, patients and care activities. Fabbri and LeFevre (2011) measured how often clinical relationships explained real and randomly generated user–patient accesses, without independently confirmed incidents. Chen and Malin (2011) analysed user communities and tested detection by inserting simulated anomalous users into real logs.

Menon et al. (2014) used collaborative filtering to learn user–patient interaction patterns from observed and latent (inferred) features. In their Hospital experiment, all records for a user had the same label. They removed raw user and patient identifiers to avoid rewarding identity memorisation, but retained cluster identifiers. Across these evaluations, detection of independently validated misuse by previously unseen real users or involving previously unseen real patients remains unestablished; tests with injected users address a different setting.

Clinical and organisational explanations can justify flagged access and reduce the cases needing review (Fabbri & LeFevre, 2011; Hedda et al., 2017). This supports evaluating legitimate exceptions and examining who bears false-alert burdens. Here, detection is measured against source labels. Human review, correction of erroneous alerts and possible group disparities are discussed in Section 5.6; those operational safeguards and outcomes were not validated by the present experiments.

Label origin and alert quality affect how detection results should be read. Hurst et al. (2022) trained supervised classifiers on aggregated UK hospital activity. Density-based screening and record checks informed the labels; the report does not establish independent investigation of every case. With anomalies positive, test accuracy was 0.9896 but positive predictive value (PPV), the proportion of positive predictions labelled positive, was 0.4486. Table 2.3 retains splits and validation results. These label and unit differences matter when interpreting the present precision and average precision (AP).

Tabassum et al. (2024) generated electronic patient record (EPR) labels with Isolation Forest (IF) and Local Outlier Factor (LOF), which flag statistically unusual records, before training classifiers. Performance against these pseudo-labels may reflect agreement with the labelling algorithms rather than detection of independently confirmed threats. Table 2.3 retains the SVM accuracy results and the source’s inconsistent IF-SVM sensitivity values.

Autoencoders can model routine behaviour without labelled examples of every threat. Recurrent autoencoders process events in sequence. Martínez Llamas et al. (2025) combined an LSTM autoencoder with Flower and FedAvg for EHR access-anomaly detection.

Senturk et al. (2025) compared vector and LSTM autoencoders trained on normal synthetic activity, using validation-based thresholds and Integrated Gradients for feature attribution. Among 200 evaluated observations, the vector model had higher anomaly recall and F1, while the LSTM produced fewer false positives. Reporting of observation construction, partitions, test feedback and explanations leaves validation independence and explanation faithfulness unresolved (Appendix A.4). The comparison was centralised, without federated learning or secure aggregation.

Federated training extends detection to data held at several clients. FedAvg combines locally trained parameters, usually weighting clients by their training-example counts (McMahan et al., 2017). In binary network-intrusion classification, Lazzarini et al. (2023) reported higher centralised accuracy and F1 than aggregated FL on both ToN_IoT and CICIDS2017; simulated clients retained class proportions. Appendix A.4 records the values. This supplies a methodological precedent outside EHR monitoring, rather than evidence of performance across heterogeneous hospitals.

Client distributions and local training budgets affect federated optimisation. McMahan et al. (2017) found that training plateaued or diverged at excessive local epochs in Shakespeare, while MNIST behaved differently. FedProx penalises movement from the current global model and was evaluated under differences in data and system capabilities (Li et al., 2020). The present design reports local budgets explicitly (Section 3.9) and varies department-biased resampling (Section 3.4), which changes client composition, pooled composition and session repetition together.

Personalisation responds to client differences by combining shared and client-specific components. FeadSeq (Guan et al., 2025) shares selected sequence-model parameters and compares FedAvg with personalised methods on system and business-process logs. It reports AP over five runs, sensitivity analyses and component ablations. Its masks select participating weights rather than cryptographically hide them, and communication is counted as shared parameters. These experiments distinguish personalisation from cryptographic protection; they do not isolate SecAgg+ or establish EHR staff-access performance.

Without anomaly ground truth, the reconstruction errors and flag counts in Martínez Llamas et al. (2025) cannot establish precision, recall or false-positive rates. Table 2.3 records the window size, reported errors, flags and threshold choices, including federated thresholds derived from training data. The present comparison evaluates supplied scenario-labelled sessions and adds a matched standard-FedAvg versus SecAgg+ condition. This changes the available evaluation evidence; the different data and units still prevent a numerical superiority claim.

Secure-aggregation protocols differ in how clients exchange information to combine updates. Bonawitz et al. (2017) presented a practical protocol. Bell et al. (2020) reduced per-client overhead by replacing complete communication graphs with sparse graphs containing fewer connections.

Bell et al.’s proofs assume that the set of corrupted clients is fixed before execution and dropout stays within specified bounds. In the semi-malicious model, the server may deviate arbitrarily after honestly collecting and committing client public keys; external public-key infrastructure is an alternative. The full technical version reports numerical parameter analyses and cryptographic-component benchmarks, with system implementation left to future work.

Li et al. (2022) described Salvia, a SecAgg(+) implementation for Flower under a semi-honest model, in which participants follow the protocol but may infer information from their observations. Salvia encrypts and authenticates client–server links. Flower 1.22.0 supports SecAgg+ (Flower Labs, n.d.), providing a common framework for comparing standard FedAvg with protected aggregation.

Aggregation can still expose information under some threat models. Ngo et al. (2024), in an arXiv preprint, analyse a passive server observing the exact update sum. They assume it can simulate training to estimate client-update averages and how entries vary together. Those estimates, the aggregate and two candidate updates may help identify which candidate a client submitted. This is statistical inference, not direct inspection of an individual update. It supports reporting protocol assumptions and visible outputs alongside utility and cost; it does not establish an attack on the present implementation.

Detection metrics must describe missed threats and false alerts. Precision–recall analysis is informative under class imbalance, but its baseline and area depend on the positive-class proportion (Davis & Goadrich, 2006; Saito & Rehmsmeier, 2015). Reconstruction loss measures input reconstruction, rather than threat identity. AP should therefore accompany recall and false-positive rates, including errors on unusual legitimate activity. Section 3.10 defines the measures; Appendix A.4 retains the implementation-specific AP/PR-AUC distinction.

Cost comparisons require an explicit measurement boundary. Training-workflow time, application-message content and prepared-input inference cover different operations (Section 3.10). They complement detection metrics without isolating cryptographic computation or measuring complete deployment latency. Practical acceptability also depends on investigation workload and end-to-end operation.

Secure aggregation returned the expected public test values within the specified numerical limits. All five valid-input controls completed four stages and accepted one aggregate each. The largest absolute error was 2.05046 × 10⁻⁵, below the 1.23978 × 10⁻⁴ limit. Appendix C.7 retains the grid, weights and boundary controls. These checks concern numerical agreement, not privacy leakage.

The corrected version passed 59 targeted cases under the original criteria, including all seven SV-05 fixtures, and 12 additional guard cases. Separately reported unit/regression testing passed 75 tests without failures, errors or skips. These counts describe different checks and should not be combined into one sample. The complete historical 101-case suite was not repeated. Appendix C.7 retains request ordering, valid controls and early-rejection details.
